title: SAFE Drugs Act of 2026
official_title: To amend the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to further regulate compounding pharmacies and outsourcing facilities, and for other purposes.
summary: Pharmacies and doctors can mix custom versions of drugs, called compounding, without FDA approval as long as they meet the conditions in Section 503A of the food and drug law. This bill adds two more conditions: a compounder who sends drugs out of State must pass on any serious adverse event report it receives and, once out-of-State shipments top 5 percent of what it compounds in a year, file an annual report; and every compounded drug label must say the drug has not been approved by the Food and Drug Administration and carry the FDA adverse-event website and phone number.
brief: Requires compounders who ship across State lines to pass on serious adverse event reports and file an annual report above a 5 percent interstate threshold, and requires every compounded drug label to state that the drug is not FDA-approved.

top_lines.headline: Adverse Event Reporting
subs: Serious adverse event reports must go to the Secretary and both States
Applies to compounders who send drug products out of State
Uses the existing federal adverse-event report content and format

top_lines.headline: Annual Interstate Report
subs: Triggered above 5 percent of annual compounded volume sent out of State
Due by January 15 each year to the Secretary and the receiving State
Lists name, address, license number, and monthly units by product type
Hospital pharmacies compounding for hospital patients are excluded

top_lines.headline: Label Warning
subs: Label must state the drug has not been approved by the FDA
Label must carry the FDA adverse-event website and phone number
Becomes one of the conditions for compounding under Section 503A

top_lines.headline: State Law Preserved
subs: Stricter or supplementary State reporting requirements are not preempted

likelihoodReason: Sponsored by a Republican with one Democratic cosponsor, and reported from the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee by Senator Cassidy with an amendment in the nature of a substitute that narrowed the bill to reporting and labeling. Opposition is likeliest from compounding pharmacists and physicians who dispense across State lines, who take on the new annual report and the adverse-event pass-through, and who would have to carry the not-approved statement on every label. The latest-action metadata places it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 524.

items.main: Requires a licensed pharmacist or physician who compounds under Section 503A and sends the product out of State to forward any serious adverse event report they receive to the Secretary, to the State where the compounding happened, and to each State the drugs are sent to.
items.detail: The report follows the content and format requirements established through guidance or under section 310.305 of title 21, Code of Federal Regulations, or any successor regulations. The requirement is written as a new subsection (d) of Section 503A, inserted after subsection (c); the existing subsections (d) Application and (e) Compounding defined are redesignated (e) and (f).

items.main: Adds an annual report for compounders who send more than 5 percent of their total annual compounded volume out of State.
items.detail: Beginning with the first calendar year that starts after enactment, the report is due not later than January 15 of each calendar year, to the Secretary and to the State the products are sent to. It must give the compounder name, address, license number and State of license, and the total units of compounded drug products by product type and by month sent to each applicable State. Section 503A already carries a 5 percent interstate figure, but on a different base: for a State that has not entered a memorandum of understanding with the Secretary, out-of-State distribution is limited to 5 percent of the total prescription orders dispensed or distributed. The new report counts 5 percent of the total annual amount of drug products compounded.

items.main: Directs the Secretary to use an information sharing system to move the reports to the Secretary and each applicable State, and excludes hospital pharmacies compounding for hospital patients.
items.detail: The bill states the information sharing system is for reducing unnecessary administrative burden. The exclusion clause says the subsection does not apply to the compounding of any drug products for hospital patients by a pharmacy located on the premises of the hospital. A rule of construction states that nothing in the section is to be construed to preempt a State or local requirement for additional, more stringent, or supplementary reporting on a drug product compounded under the section.

items.main: Adds a label requirement to Section 503A(b)(3): the label must state that the medication has been compounded for dispensing to an individual patient and has not been approved by the Food and Drug Administration.
items.detail: The label must also carry www.fda.gov/medwatch and 1-800-FDA-1088, or any successor website or telephone number, to facilitate adverse event reporting, plus any other information the Secretary prescribes by order. The two existing subparagraphs of Section 503A(b)(3) are repunctuated to take the new subparagraph (C).

underreported.summary: Places the new label statement inside Section 503A(b)(3), the paragraph that lists the conditions a drug product must meet to be compounded under the section. Section 503A(a) makes the exemption from the drug approval, prescription-labeling, and manufacturing-practice requirements conditional on meeting the requirements of the section, and (b)(3) opens with the words a drug product may be compounded under subsection (a) only if. A label missing the statement or the adverse-event contacts would therefore fail an eligibility condition, not just a disclosure rule.
underreported.why_unreported: The section is captioned Labeling, which reads as a disclosure duty. Its placement in the eligibility paragraph ties label content to whether the compounded drug qualifies for the Section 503A exemption at all.

underreported.summary: Sets the annual interstate report trigger at more than 5 percent of the total annual amount of drug products compounded by the pharmacist or physician.
underreported.why_unreported: Section 503A already contains a 5 percent interstate figure, measured against the total prescription orders dispensed or distributed and applying only in States that have not entered a memorandum of understanding with the Secretary. The two figures share a number but not a base or a trigger condition.

gaps: The bill requires an annual interstate report and an adverse-event pass-through but states no consequence for failing to file either one.
The bill directs the Secretary to use an information sharing system to carry the reports to each State, but does not say who builds it, what it must do, or by when.

added: New subsection (d)(1) of Section 503A of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 U.S.C. 353a) — serious adverse event reports received by a compounder who ships out of State must be forwarded to the Secretary, the compounding State, and each receiving State

New paragraph (d)(2) of Section 503A — annual interstate dispensing report, due January 15, for compounders sending more than 5 percent of annual compounded volume out of State, with a hospital pharmacy exclusion and a non-preemption rule of construction
New subparagraph (b)(3)(C) of Section 503A — label must state the drug is compounded and not FDA-approved, and must carry the FDA adverse-event website and telephone number
modified: Section 503A of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 U.S.C. 353a) — existing subsections (d) and (e) redesignated as (e) and (f) to make room for the new reporting subsection
